55	
56	// ScanOptions configures which scanners to run
57	type ScanOptions struct {
58		// Categories is what the scan looks for and, per category, which tools
59		// run it (§3.86). Uses reads it.
60		Categories config.ScanCategories
61		// Tools is every tool's settings: where it runs from, and its own options.
62		Tools config.ScanTools
63		// TrivyServer is the address a scan sends Trivy to, and empty unless the
64		// client-server mode is on: the address is kept in the config while the
65		// mode is off, and a scan must not see it then. OptionsFromConfig resolves
66		// it once, so no stage re-reads the switch.
67		TrivyServer string
68		// Detected is a detection already made — the router's, shared by every
69		// view — so a scan does not probe the machine again. Nil detects, which is
70		// what a caller with no report yet gets. A tool that disappeared between
71		// that detection and the scan fails at its stage, with the stage's message.
72		Detected *Report
73	
74		// Forge is the platform this context targets, and it is what decides
75		// whether a repository is graded at all: a GitHub context grades its GitHub
76		// repositories and nothing else (§3.42). The scan resolves that per target
77		// rather than per batch, because one batch holds repositories with
78		// different remotes.
79		Forge config.ForgeConfig
80		// LoadForgeToken is called only for a repository whose remote is the
81		// configured forge, so one of another host never reaches the secret store.
82		// It runs on a scan goroutine, like the clone's tokenLoader.
83		LoadForgeToken func() string
84		// OnProgress is an optional callback invoked at each stage transition.
85		// It is called from scan goroutines; implementations must be thread-safe.
86		OnProgress func(ProgressUpdate)
87	}
88	
89	// Finding represents a single security finding
90	type Finding struct {
91		ID          string        `json:"id"`
92		Title       string        `json:"title"`
93		Description string        `json:"description"`
94		Severity    SeverityLevel `json:"severity"`
95		Source      string        `json:"source"` // "trivy" or "gitleaks"
96		File        string        `json:"file"`
97		Line        int           `json:"line"`
98		Match       string        `json:"match,omitempty"`       // For secrets
99		Fingerprint string        `json:"fingerprint,omitempty"` // Gitleaks fingerprint for .gitleaksignore
100		PkgName     string        `json:"pkg_name,omitempty"`    // For vulnerabilities
101		Version     string        `json:"version,omitempty"`
102		FixedIn     string        `json:"fixed_in,omitempty"`
103		Resolution  string        `json:"resolution,omitempty"`  // Recommended fix steps
104		References  []string      `json:"references,omitempty"`  // Links to advisories or documentation
105		FixCommand  string        `json:"fix_command,omitempty"` // Suggested command to run
106		// Class and Ecosystem say what kind of package a vulnerability sits in:
107		// Trivy's Result.Class (os-pkgs or lang-pkgs) and Result.Type (alpine,
108		// debian, gomod, npm...). The class decides the fix — a base image bump
109		// clears an os-pkgs CVE and does nothing for a lang-pkgs one. Both are
110		// empty on results cached before they were recorded, which reads as
111		// "unknown" and is never counted as either class.
112		Class     string `json:"class,omitempty"`
113		Ecosystem string `json:"ecosystem,omitempty"`
114		// EndLine, Message and Status belong to a misconfiguration (§3.78). Trivy
115		// has always reported them and they were dropped when the Finding was
116		// built, which left a caller knowing where a faulty block starts and not
117		// where it ends — enough to read, not enough to replace.
118		//
119		// EndLine is the last line of that block, Line being its first. Message is
120		// this instance's own wording ("Specify at least 1 USER command") where
121		// Description carries the rule's generic text, and Status is what Trivy
122		// concluded for the rule on this target.
123		//
124		// All three are empty on a result cached before they were recorded, which
125		// reads as "unknown" — an EndLine of zero is never a line number — and they
126		// reappear at the next scan. Same convention as Class and Ecosystem above,
127		// and no cache migration for the same reason.
128		EndLine int    `json:"end_line,omitempty"`
129		Message string `json:"message,omitempty"`
130		Status  string `json:"status,omitempty"`
131		// Job and ScriptLine are where a CI finding sits inside the pipeline
132		// (§3.42). plumber grades the configuration GitLab derives from the
133		// repository — includes and components resolved server-side — so a finding
134		// is about a job the repository very often does not contain, and its own
135		// file link points at the `include:` entry that brought it in rather than
136		// at the offending line.
137		//
138		// These two are the anchors that survive that: the job the control was
139		// looking at, and, on the controls that read a script, the offending line
140		// verbatim. Both are empty on the controls that are about the project
141		// rather than the pipeline — branch protection, approval rules — and on
142		// those about an include, which name nothing at all.
143		//
144		// ScriptLine is not a secret and must not become one: it is the pipeline's
145		// own source, already visible to anyone who can read the repository. The
146		// MCP `finding` type declares its fields one by one, so nothing here
147		// reaches it without being added there deliberately.
148		Job        string `json:"job,omitempty"`
149		ScriptLine string `json:"script_line,omitempty"`
150		// IaCType is the dialect a misconfiguration was found in: Trivy's
151		// Result.Type — "dockerfile", "kubernetes", "helm", "terraform",
152		// "cloudformation"… — and "kubernetes" for a schema finding (§3.80). It is
153		// what tells a Deployment's KSV rule from a Dockerfile's DS rule without
154		// reading the file name, and what the fix catalog checks before touching a
155		// file: a finding in a Helm template points at a template, not at YAML it
156		// can edit.
157		//
158		// Empty on anything that is not a misconfiguration, and on a result cached
159		// before it was recorded — "unknown", like Class and Ecosystem.
160		IaCType string `json:"iac_type,omitempty"`
161	}
162	
163	// SeverityCounts holds counts by severity level
164	type SeverityCounts struct {
165		Critical int `json:"critical"`
166		High     int `json:"high"`
167		Medium   int `json:"medium"`
168		Low      int `json:"low"`
169		Unknown  int `json:"unknown"`
170	}
171	
172	// Result represents the aggregated scan results
173	type Result struct {
174		Target      string         `json:"target"`
175		TargetType  TargetType     `json:"target_type"`
176		StartTime   time.Time      `json:"start_time"`
177		EndTime     time.Time      `json:"end_time"`
178		Duration    time.Duration  `json:"duration"`
179		Counts      SeverityCounts `json:"counts"`       // CVE counts by severity
180		SecretCount int            `json:"secret_count"` // Total secrets found (gitleaks + trivy)
181		// SecretsScanned tells "no secret was found" apart from "no one looked".
182		// A secrets stage can fail to run for three reasons — the option is off,
183		// the tool is missing, the stage errored — and in all three cases a
184		// counter stuck at zero would say "this target is clean" about a scan
185		// that never looked at it. It is the same principle as missingToolErrors
186		// below (§1.3 D20), carried through to what the views display.
187		SecretsScanned bool `json:"secrets_scanned"`
188		LicenseCount   int  `json:"license_count"`   // Total license issues found
189		MisconfigCount int  `json:"misconfig_count"` // Total misconfigurations found
190		// MisconfigScanned tells "no misconfiguration was found" apart from "no one
191		// looked", exactly as SecretsScanned does two fields up. The category has
192		// two stages — Trivy's security rules and kubeconform's schema validation —
193		// and either can be cut by the option, by a missing tool, or fail; in all of
194		// those a counter stuck at zero would call a target clean that nothing ever
195		// read.
196		MisconfigScanned bool `json:"misconfig_scanned"`
197		// MisconfigWorst is the highest severity among the misconfigurations, and it
198		// is what colours the column.
199		//
200		// One column rather than four: the C/H/M/L counters beside it count
201		// vulnerabilities only, and splitting misconfigurations the same way would
202		// spend sixteen cells in the narrowest table of the application answering a
203		// question nobody asks of them — a misconfiguration backlog is read whole,
204		// not severity by severity, and what one wants from the list is whether
205		// there is a CRITICAL in it. Empty when there are none.
206		MisconfigWorst SeverityLevel `json:"misconfig_worst,omitempty"`
207		CIIssueCount   int           `json:"ci_issue_count"` // Total CI-configuration issues found
208		Findings       []Finding     `json:"findings"`
209		Errors         []string      `json:"errors,omitempty"`
210	
211		// CIScanned tells "this pipeline was graded" apart from "no one looked",
212		// exactly as SecretsScanned does one field up: the stage can fail to run
213		// four ways — the option is off, plumber is absent, the repository is not
214		// this context's forge, or the run errored — and in all four a letter would
215		// be a claim nobody made.
216		CIScanned bool `json:"ci_scanned"`
217		// CIScore is the letter, and it is **empty on a withheld run**. plumber
218		// writes one anyway, and it flatters: on the reference fixture the degraded
219		// run reads B/79 where the complete run reads E/30, because a control that
220		// did not run found nothing.
221		CIScore string `json:"ci_score,omitempty"`
222		// CIPoints is finalPoints out of 100, a float — see PlumberReport.Points.
223		CIPoints float64 `json:"ci_points,omitempty"`
224		// CIWithheld is a run that could not conclude, and CIReasons is what it
225		// could not collect. Together they are the `?` of the CI column.
226		CIWithheld bool     `json:"ci_withheld,omitempty"`
227		CIReasons  []string `json:"ci_reasons,omitempty"`
228		// CIMissing is a repository with no pipeline at all, which is not a bad
229		// score — it is the absence of the thing being scored.
230		CIMissing bool `json:"ci_missing,omitempty"`
231	
232		// K8sUnrendered are the Helm charts and Kustomize overlays the schema
233		// stage could not validate because nothing rendered them (§3.80). Not an
234		// error — the scan did all it could — and not "clean" either: it is what
235		// keeps "nothing was found there" apart from "nobody looked there".
236		K8sUnrendered []string `json:"k8s_unrendered,omitempty"`
237	}
238	
239	// CIVerdict is what this scan can say about the pipeline's grade, for the cache
240	// and the column: nil when nothing graded it, the letter otherwise.
241	//
242	// It is the only calculation of the verdict, on SecretVerdict's model and for
243	// its reason — there were two of those, written the same way, and both became
244	// wrong on the same day (§3.12). A withheld run answers nil rather than its
245	// letter: nobody concluded, so nobody may be quoted.
246	func (r *Result) CIVerdict() *string {
247		if !r.CIScanned || r.CIWithheld || r.CIScore == "" {
248			return nil
249		}
250		score := r.CIScore
251		return &score
252	}
253	
254	// MisconfigSummary is what a scan concluded about misconfigurations: how many
255	// there are, how bad the worst one is, and how much of the target no stage
256	// could read at all.
257	//
258	// Unrendered is len(K8sUnrendered), carried here because the caches keep this
259	// summary and not the whole result. A Helm chart nobody rendered is not a clean
260	// chart: a row printing "0" for a repository of charts would be exactly the
261	// confusion SecretsScanned exists to prevent, one category over.
262	type MisconfigSummary struct {
263		Count      int           `json:"count"`
264		Worst      SeverityLevel `json:"worst,omitempty"`
265		Unrendered int           `json:"unrendered,omitempty"`
266	}
267	
268	// Total, WorstSeverity and UnrenderedCount read a summary that may be nil,
269	// which is the state "nobody looked". They exist so a caller can hand the three
270	// numbers to internal/ui/theme without unwrapping the pointer first: that
271	// package takes plain values on purpose — it does not import this one, which is
272	// also why SeverityTextStyle takes a string.
273	func (m *MisconfigSummary) Total() int {
274		if m == nil {
275			return 0
276		}
277		return m.Count
278	}
279	
280	// WorstSeverity is the highest severity present, as the string theme wants.
281	func (m *MisconfigSummary) WorstSeverity() string {
282		if m == nil {
283			return ""
284		}
285		return string(m.Worst)
286	}
287	
288	// UnrenderedCount is how many charts or overlays nothing rendered.
289	func (m *MisconfigSummary) UnrenderedCount() int {
290		if m == nil {
291			return 0
292		}
293		return m.Unrendered
294	}
295	
296	// MisconfigVerdict is what this scan can say about misconfigurations, for the
297	// caches and the column: nil when no stage looked, a summary otherwise.
298	//
299	// Third of its kind after SecretVerdict and CIVerdict, and the only calculation
300	// — the workspaces list, the security inventory and the images list all read
301	// this one rather than counting findings again for themselves.
302	func (r *Result) MisconfigVerdict() *MisconfigSummary {
303		if !r.MisconfigScanned {
304			return nil
305		}
306		return &MisconfigSummary{
307			Count:      r.MisconfigCount,
308			Worst:      r.MisconfigWorst,
309			Unrendered: len(r.K8sUnrendered),
310		}
311	}
312	
313	// severityRank orders the severities so two of them can be compared.
314	//
315	// Unknown ranks above nothing and below LOW: a rule whose severity the tool did
316	// not state must not outrank one that did, and must not be mistaken for the
317	// empty value that means "there are none".
318	func severityRank(s SeverityLevel) int {
319		switch s {
320		case SeverityCritical:
321			return 5
322		case SeverityHigh:
323			return 4
324		case SeverityMedium:
325			return 3
326		case SeverityLow:
327			return 2
328		case SeverityUnknown:
329			return 1
330		default:
331			return 0
332		}
333	}
334	
335	// WorseSeverity returns whichever of the two is higher. Exported because the
336	// workspaces list folds the summaries of the repositories under a directory,
337	// and that fold must order severities the same way this package does.
338	func WorseSeverity(a, b SeverityLevel) SeverityLevel {
339		if severityRank(b) > severityRank(a) {
340			return b
341		}
342		return a
343	}
344	
345	// recordStageError puts a stage's failure where it can be found.
346	//
347	// The result carries it for the caches and the callers; the **log** carries the
348	// detail, because the views do not print a tool's stderr any more — Rule 128's
349	// arrangement, which this package was not part of: a stage that failed appended
350	// to result.Errors and logged nothing, so the only copy of the reason was on
351	// screen, in a panel that replaced the findings. The footer now says to look in
352	// the log, and this is what makes that true.
353	func recordStageError(result *Result, stage string, err error) {
354		log.Printf("ERROR [scan/%s] stage failed: %v", stage, err)
355		result.Errors = append(result.Errors, fmt.Sprintf("%s: %v", stage, err))
356	}
357	
358	// CountFindings aggregates findings into separate counters by category and
359	// severity. Vulnerabilities are counted by severity into Counts; secrets,
360	// licenses and misconfigurations into their dedicated fields.
361	//
362	// The category comes from Categorize, which the results tabs also use — these
363	// counters and the tab labels are the same numbers, and used to be computed by
364	// two rules that disagreed (see category.go).
365	func (r *Result) CountFindings() {
366		r.Counts = SeverityCounts{}
367		r.SecretCount = 0
368		r.LicenseCount = 0
369		r.MisconfigCount = 0
370		r.MisconfigWorst = ""
371		r.CIIssueCount = 0
372		for _, f := range r.Findings {
373			switch Categorize(f) {
374			case CategorySecret:
375				r.SecretCount++
376			case CategoryLicense:
377				r.LicenseCount++
378			case CategoryMisconfiguration:
379				r.MisconfigCount++
380				r.MisconfigWorst = WorseSeverity(r.MisconfigWorst, f.Severity)
381			case CategoryCIScore:
382				r.CIIssueCount++
383			case CategoryVulnerability:
384				r.countBySeverity(f.Severity)
385			}
386		}
387	}
388	
389	// countBySeverity adds one vulnerability to the severity histogram.
390	func (r *Result) countBySeverity(severity SeverityLevel) {
391		switch severity {
392		case SeverityCritical:
393			r.Counts.Critical++
394		case SeverityHigh:
395			r.Counts.High++
396		case SeverityMedium:
397			r.Counts.Medium++
398		case SeverityLow:
399			r.Counts.Low++
400		default:
401			r.Counts.Unknown++
402		}
403	}
404	
405	// SecretVerdict is what this scan can say about secrets, for the caches and the
406	// columns that show a verdict rather than a count: nil when no stage looked,
407	// false when one looked and found nothing, true when one found something.
408	//
409	// It is the only verdict calculation in the application. There used to be
410	// two, both written as "a finding whose Source is gitleaks", and both became
411	// wrong the day Trivy started finding secrets too: a repo whose only secrets
412	// were Trivy's read as clean. SecretCount comes from Categorize, which is
413	// the only classifier (§3.11).
414	func (r *Result) SecretVerdict() *bool {
415		if !r.SecretsScanned {
416			return nil
417		}
418		found := r.SecretCount > 0
419		return &found
420	}
421	
422	// TotalFindings returns the total number of findings across all types
423	func (r *Result) TotalFindings() int {
424		return r.Counts.Critical + r.Counts.High + r.Counts.Medium + r.Counts.Low + r.Counts.Unknown +
425			r.SecretCount + r.LicenseCount + r.MisconfigCount + r.CIIssueCount
426	}
427	
428	// ToolSource indicates how a tool is available
429	type ToolSource string
430	
431	const (
432		ToolSourceNone   ToolSource = "none"
433		ToolSourceBinary ToolSource = "binary"
434		// ToolSourceContainer runs the tool from an image, through whichever engine
435		// is configured. It used to be ToolSourceDocker = "docker", which baked the
436		// engine's name into a type the UI reads (§3.67). The rename is internal
437		// only: this value is never serialised, and the configuration already spells
438		// the same choice engine-neutrally (config.ToolSourceImage = "image").
439		ToolSourceContainer ToolSource = "container"
440	)
441	
442	// Default images for the container-sourced tools
443	const (
444		DefaultTrivyImage    = "aquasec/trivy"
445		DefaultGitleaksImage = "zricethezav/gitleaks"
446		DefaultPlumberImage  = "getplumber/plumber"
447	)
448	
449	// imageIsLocal verifies that the engine already holds an image.
450	func imageIsLocal(image string) bool {
451		cmd := exec.Command(engine.Current().Binary, "images", "-q", image) //nolint:gosec // the binary is a declared engine name or a configured path
452		output, err := cmd.Output()
453		if err != nil {
454			return false
455		}
456		// If output is not empty, image exists
457		return len(output) > 0
458	}
459	
460	// Scanner performs security scans using multiple tools
461	type Scanner struct {
462		options ScanOptions
463		deps    Report
464	}
465	
466	// NewScanner creates a new scanner with the given options, on the detection
467	// they carry, or on a fresh one when they carry none.
468	func NewScanner(opts ScanOptions) *Scanner {
469		if opts.Detected != nil {
470			return newScannerWithDeps(opts, *opts.Detected)
471		}
472		return newScannerWithDeps(opts, Detect(opts.Tools))
473	}
474	
475	// newScannerWithDeps builds a scanner against a known set of tools. Detection
476	// probes the machine it runs on, so tests state the availability they mean
477	// instead of inheriting the developer's installation.
478	func newScannerWithDeps(opts ScanOptions, deps Report) *Scanner {
479		return &Scanner{options: opts, deps: deps}
480	}
481	
482	// spec is how one tool is handed to its builder: where detection found it,
483	// plus what the context adds — its extra arguments, and Trivy's rules file.
484	func (s *Scanner) spec(id ToolID) ToolSpec {
485		spec := s.deps.Spec(id)
486		set := s.options.Tools.Tool(string(id))
487		spec.Args = set.Args
488		if id == ToolTrivy {
489			spec.Config = set.Config
490		}
491		return spec
492	}
493	
494	// runs reports whether one category's tool runs on this target: the settings
495	// ask for it, it applies to the target, and it is there.
496	func (s *Scanner) runs(cat CategoryID, tool ToolID, targetType TargetType) bool {
497		return s.wants(cat, tool, targetType) && s.deps.Available(tool)
498	}
499	
500	// wants is runs without the availability: what the settings ask of this target.
501	func (s *Scanner) wants(cat CategoryID, tool ToolID, targetType TargetType) bool {
502		if !Uses(s.options.Categories, cat, tool) {
503			return false
504		}
505		for _, c := range categoryTable {
506			if c.ID != cat {
507				continue
508			}
509			for _, ct := range c.Tools {
510				if ct.Tool == tool {
511					// What a Trivy server cannot do is not done, rather than
512					// forced off in the configuration: the tick survives the
513					// server being switched off again (§3.86).
514					if tool == ToolTrivy && !ct.Server && s.options.TrivyServer != "" {
515						return false
516					}
517					return ct.Applies(targetType)
518				}
519			}
520		}
521		return false
522	}
523	
524	// missingToolErrors reports the tools the caller asked for that cannot run
525	// because they are neither installed nor available as an image — one error per
526	// tool, read off the tables, so every tool is reported the same way (plumber
527	// was not, until §3.86).
528	//
529	// A tool that does not apply to the target type is not missing anything:
530	// gitleaks scans a working tree, so a secret scan of an image skips it for a
531	// reason that has nothing to do with what the machine has installed.
532	//
533	// A renderer (helm, kustomize) is not reported here: without it the stage still
534	// runs, and names each chart or overlay it could not validate
535	// (Result.K8sUnrendered) — which says more than one line per scan would.
536	func (s *Scanner) missingToolErrors(targetType TargetType) []string {
537		var errs []string
538		for _, tool := range toolTable {
539			if s.deps.Available(tool.ID) || !s.wantsAnywhere(tool.ID, targetType) {
540				continue
541			}
542			errs = append(errs, fmt.Sprintf("%s: not available — %s. Install %s or pull %s",
543				tool.Binary, tool.Lost, tool.Binary, s.deps.Status(tool.ID).Image))
544		}
545		return errs
546	}
547	
548	// wantsAnywhere reports whether some category asks this target for the tool,
549	// leaving out the renderers, whose absence the stage reports itself.
550	func (s *Scanner) wantsAnywhere(tool ToolID, targetType TargetType) bool {
551		for _, cat := range categoryTable {
552			for _, ct := range cat.Tools {
553				if ct.Tool == tool && ct.DependsOn == "" && s.wants(cat.ID, tool, targetType) {
554					return true
555				}
556			}
557		}
558		return false
559	}
560	
561	// ErrTrivyUnavailable is returned by ScanRemoteImage when Trivy cannot be run.
562	var ErrTrivyUnavailable = errors.New("trivy is not available")
563	
564	// ScanRemoteImage scans an image read from its registry, without pulling it
565	// into the local engine: the vulnerability stage only, with the options this
566	// scanner was built with (server, ignore-unfixed, ignore-EOL).
567	//
568	// It exists to measure a base image bump. A candidate is not something the user
569	// owns, so it must not land in the engine's storage, and only the CVE counts of
570	// it matter — secrets and misconfigurations describe the user's own layers, not
571	// the base's.
572	func (s *Scanner) ScanRemoteImage(ctx context.Context, image string) (*Result, error) {
573		if !s.deps.Available(ToolTrivy) {
574			return nil, ErrTrivyUnavailable
575		}
576		if err := checkRulesFile("trivy", s.spec(ToolTrivy).Config); err != nil {
577			return nil, err
578		}
579		result := &Result{
580			Target:     image,
581			TargetType: TargetImage,
582			StartTime:  time.Now(),
583			Findings:   []Finding{},
584			Errors:     []string{},
585		}
586		tc, err := trivyRemoteImageArgs(image, s.spec(ToolTrivy), s.options.TrivyServer, s.options.Tools.Trivy.IgnoreUnfixed, s.options.Tools.Trivy.IgnoreEOL)
587		if err != nil {
588			return nil, err
589		}
590		log.Printf("Running: %s", tc.String())
591		findings, err := runTrivy(ctx, tc, nil)
592		if err != nil {
593			return nil, err
594		}
595		result.Findings = findings
596		result.EndTime = time.Now()
597		result.Duration = result.EndTime.Sub(result.StartTime)
598		result.CountFindings()
599		return result, nil
600	}
601	
602	// Scan performs a security scan on the target, running all enabled stages in parallel.
603	func (s *Scanner) Scan(ctx context.Context, target string, targetType TargetType) (*Result, error) {
604		result := &Result{
605			Target:     target,
606			TargetType: targetType,
607			StartTime:  time.Now(),
608			Findings:   []Finding{},
609			Errors:     []string{},
610		}
611	
612		notify := func(update ProgressUpdate) {
613			if s.options.OnProgress != nil {
614				s.options.OnProgress(update)
615			}
616		}
617	
618		// A stage whose tool is missing is not started at all, so it leaves neither a
619		// finding nor an error behind — and a result with neither is indistinguishable
620		// from a clean scan. Recording the reason up front is what stops "nothing
621		// looked at this image" being reported as "this image is fine" (§1.3 D20).
622		result.Errors = append(result.Errors, s.missingToolErrors(targetType)...)
623	
624		// mu guards writes to result (Findings, Errors) from concurrent goroutines
625		var mu sync.Mutex
626	
627		eg, egCtx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)
628	
629		// Vuln scan (Trivy)
630		if s.runs(CategoryIDVuln, ToolTrivy, targetType) {
631			eg.Go(func() error {
632				notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "vuln", Label: "Vulnerabilities", Status: StageRunning})
633				progressFn := func(detail string) {
634					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "vuln", Label: "Vulnerabilities", Status: StageRunning, Detail: detail})
635				}
636				cmd := GetTrivyCommand(target, targetType, false, s.spec(ToolTrivy), s.options.TrivyServer, s.options.Tools.Trivy.IgnoreUnfixed, s.options.Tools.Trivy.IgnoreEOL)
637				log.Printf("Running: %s", cmd)
638				findings, err := RunTrivy(egCtx, target, targetType, false, s.spec(ToolTrivy), s.options.TrivyServer, s.options.Tools.Trivy.IgnoreUnfixed, s.options.Tools.Trivy.IgnoreEOL, progressFn)
639				mu.Lock()
640				defer mu.Unlock()
641				if err != nil {
642					recordStageError(result, "trivy vuln", err)
643					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "vuln", Label: "Vulnerabilities", Status: StageError, Detail: err.Error()})
644				} else {
645					result.Findings = append(result.Findings, findings...)
646					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "vuln", Label: "Vulnerabilities", Status: StageDone})
647				}
648				return nil
649			})
650		}
651	
652		// License scan (Trivy, directory only)
653		if s.runs(CategoryIDLicense, ToolTrivy, targetType) {
654			eg.Go(func() error {
655				notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "license", Label: "Licenses", Status: StageRunning})
656				progressFn := func(detail string) {
657					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "license", Label: "Licenses", Status: StageRunning, Detail: detail})
658				}
659				cmd := GetTrivyCommand(target, targetType, true, s.spec(ToolTrivy), s.options.TrivyServer, s.options.Tools.Trivy.IgnoreUnfixed, s.options.Tools.Trivy.IgnoreEOL)
660				log.Printf("Running: %s", cmd)
661				findings, err := RunTrivy(egCtx, target, targetType, true, s.spec(ToolTrivy), s.options.TrivyServer, s.options.Tools.Trivy.IgnoreUnfixed, s.options.Tools.Trivy.IgnoreEOL, progressFn)
662				mu.Lock()
663				defer mu.Unlock()
664				if err != nil {
665					recordStageError(result, "trivy license", err)
666					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "license", Label: "Licenses", Status: StageError})
667				} else {
668					result.Findings = append(result.Findings, findings...)
669					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "license", Label: "Licenses", Status: StageDone})
670				}
671				return nil
672			})
673		}
674	
675		// CI configuration score (plumber, directories only). An image has no
676		// pipeline, so there is nothing to grade and the tab is empty on one.
677		//
678		// The target decides, not the batch: ciOptions reads this repository's own
679		// remote and refuses one that is not this context's forge.
680		if ciOpts, ok := s.ciOptions(target, targetType); ok {
681			opts := ciOpts
682			eg.Go(func() error {
683				notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "ci", Label: "CI score", Status: StageRunning})
684				progressFn := func(detail string) {
685					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "ci", Label: "CI score", Status: StageRunning, Detail: detail})
686				}
687				log.Printf("Running: %s", GetPlumberCommand(target, s.spec(ToolPlumber), opts))
688				report, err := RunPlumber(egCtx, target, s.spec(ToolPlumber), opts, progressFn)
689				mu.Lock()
690				defer mu.Unlock()
691				if err != nil {
692					recordStageError(result, "plumber", err)
693					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "ci", Label: "CI score", Status: StageError, Detail: err.Error()})
694					return nil
695				}
696				// CIScanned is written by a stage that succeeds, exactly as
697				// SecretsScanned is — a withheld run counts as having looked, which
698				// is why it is set here and Withheld is carried beside it rather
699				// than instead of it.
700				result.CIScanned = true
701				result.CIScore = report.Score
702				result.CIPoints = report.Points
703				result.CIWithheld = report.Withheld
704				result.CIReasons = report.Reasons
705				result.CIMissing = report.CIMissing
706				result.Findings = append(result.Findings, report.Findings...)
707				notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "ci", Label: "CI score", Status: StageDone})
708				return nil
709			})
710		}
711	
712		// Kubernetes schema validation (kubeconform, directories only). An image
713		// holds no manifests anyone applies. It belongs to Misconfiguration, beside
714		// Trivy's security rules (§3.86).
715		if s.runs(CategoryIDMisconfig, ToolKubeconform, targetType) {
716			eg.Go(func() error {
717				s.runKubeconformStage(egCtx, target, result, &mu, notify)
718				return nil
719			})
720		}
721	
722		// Misconfig scan (Trivy)
723		if s.runs(CategoryIDMisconfig, ToolTrivy, targetType) {
724			eg.Go(func() error {
725				notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "misconfig", Label: "Misconfigurations", Status: StageRunning})
726				progressFn := func(detail string) {
727					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "misconfig", Label: "Misconfigurations", Status: StageRunning, Detail: detail})
728				}
729				findings, err := RunTrivyMisconfig(egCtx, target, targetType, s.spec(ToolTrivy), s.options.TrivyServer, s.options.Tools.Trivy.IgnoreEOL, progressFn)
730				mu.Lock()
731				defer mu.Unlock()
732				if err != nil {
733					recordStageError(result, "trivy misconfig", err)
734					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "misconfig", Label: "Misconfigurations", Status: StageError})
735				} else {
736					result.Findings = append(result.Findings, findings...)
737					// A stage that succeeds is what makes the verdict known, as in
738					// the two secret stages below: one that fails says nothing, and
739					// certainly not "clean".
740					result.MisconfigScanned = true
741					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "misconfig", Label: "Misconfigurations", Status: StageDone})
742				}
743				return nil
744			})
745		}
746	
747		// Secret scan (Gitleaks, directory only)
748		if s.runs(CategoryIDSecret, ToolGitleaks, targetType) {
749			eg.Go(func() error {
750				notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "secret", Label: "Secrets (Gitleaks)", Status: StageRunning})
751				progressFn := func(detail string) {
752					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "secret", Label: "Secrets (Gitleaks)", Status: StageRunning, Detail: detail})
753				}
754				cmd := GetGitleaksCommand(target, s.spec(ToolGitleaks), s.options.Tools.Gitleaks.History, s.options.Tools.Gitleaks.Config)
755				log.Printf("Running: %s", cmd)
756				findings, err := RunGitleaks(egCtx, target, s.spec(ToolGitleaks), s.options.Tools.Gitleaks.History, s.options.Tools.Gitleaks.Config, progressFn)
757				mu.Lock()
758				defer mu.Unlock()
759				if err != nil {
760					recordStageError(result, "gitleaks", err)
761					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "secret", Label: "Secrets (Gitleaks)", Status: StageError})
762				} else {
763					result.Findings = append(result.Findings, findings...)
764					// A stage that succeeds is what makes the verdict known;
765					// one that fails says nothing, and certainly not "clean".
766					result.SecretsScanned = true
767					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "secret", Label: "Secrets (Gitleaks)", Status: StageDone})
768				}
769				return nil
770			})
771		}
772	
773		// Secret scan (Trivy). Both target types, unlike Gitleaks: this is what
774		// gives an image scan a secret stage at all (see the category table).
775		if s.runs(CategoryIDSecret, ToolTrivy, targetType) {
776			eg.Go(func() error {
777				notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "trivy-secret", Label: "Secrets (Trivy)", Status: StageRunning})
778				progressFn := func(detail string) {
779					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "trivy-secret", Label: "Secrets (Trivy)", Status: StageRunning, Detail: detail})
780				}
781				cmd := GetTrivySecretCommand(target, targetType, s.spec(ToolTrivy), s.options.TrivyServer)
782				log.Printf("Running: %s", cmd)
783				findings, err := RunTrivySecret(egCtx, target, targetType, s.spec(ToolTrivy), s.options.TrivyServer, progressFn)
784				mu.Lock()
785				defer mu.Unlock()
786				if err != nil {
787					recordStageError(result, "trivy secret", err)
788					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "trivy-secret", Label: "Secrets (Trivy)", Status: StageError})
789				} else {
790					result.Findings = append(result.Findings, findings...)
791					result.SecretsScanned = true
792					notify(ProgressUpdate{Stage: "trivy-secret", Label: "Secrets (Trivy)", Status: StageDone})
793				}
794				return nil
795			})
796		}
797	
798		// All goroutines return nil, so eg.Wait() never returns an error
799		_ = eg.Wait()
800	
801		result.EndTime = time.Now()
802		result.Duration = result.EndTime.Sub(result.StartTime)
803		result.CountFindings()
804	
805		return result, nil
806	}

1	// Package dockerfile reads the base images a Dockerfile builds on, and where in
2	// the file each one is written — and, for the build-context check (§3.81), what
3	// each stage copies in from the context.
4	//
5	// It exists for the security remediation (§3.2): a scan says which packages are
6	// vulnerable, and the Dockerfile is where the base image that carries them is
7	// named. Every image it reports comes with the byte range that spells it, so a
8	// later edit replaces those bytes and nothing else — comments, line endings and
9	// the rest of the file are never re-serialized.
10	//
11	// It is a reader, not a validator. It does not run the instructions, does not
12	// know about --build-arg overrides, and a Dockerfile it cannot make sense of
13	// yields fewer stages rather than an error.
14	package dockerfile
15	
16	import (
17		"encoding/json"
18		"path"
19		"regexp"
20		"strings"
21	
22		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/patch"
23	)

25	// Span is patch.Span: a range of bytes, End exclusive. It is spelled here as
26	// well so a reader of this file does not have to go looking, and because every
27	// span this parser produces exists to be handed to patch.Rewrite.
28	type Span = patch.Span
29	
30	// Kind says what a FROM instruction names.
31	type Kind int
32

34		// KindImage is an image reference, resolved or not.
35		KindImage Kind = iota
36		// KindScratch is `FROM scratch`: the empty image, nothing to scan or bump.
37		KindScratch
38		// KindStage is a FROM that names an earlier stage of the same file.
39		KindStage
40	)
41	
42	// Stage is one FROM instruction.
43	type Stage struct {
44		// Line is the 1-based line of the FROM keyword.
45		Line int
46		// Name is the `AS name` of the stage, empty if it has none.
47		Name string
48		// Platform is the --platform flag as written (possibly a variable).
49		Platform string
50		Kind     Kind
51		// Written is the image token exactly as it appears after FROM, so a view
52		// can show `${BASE}` next to what it resolves to.
53		Written string
54		// Image is the reference once build args are substituted. Empty for a
55		// scratch or stage FROM, and when Unresolved says why it could not be.
56		Image      string
57		Unresolved string
58		// Span is where the image is spelled, and Editable says whether replacing
59		// those bytes changes this stage's image. When the reference comes from an
60		// ARG default, Span is that default's value in the ARG line: the one place
61		// the image is actually written. Several stages can share it.
62		Span         Span
63		Editable     bool
64		NoEditReason string
65		// Copies are the stage's COPY and ADD instructions, in file order.
66		Copies []Copy
67	}
68	
69	// Copy is one COPY or ADD instruction (§3.81).
70	//
71	// It is read for one question — does this instruction take the whole build
72	// context — so it keeps what answers it and nothing else: where the sources come
73	// from, what they are, and whether a flag narrows them.
74	type Copy struct {
75		// Line and EndLine are the 1-based lines the instruction spans, the escape
76		// character's continuations included.
77		Line    int
78		EndLine int
79		// Keyword is COPY or ADD, uppercased.
80		Keyword string
81		// From is the --from flag's value: another stage or an image, not the
82		// build context. Empty when the sources come from the context.
83		From string
84		// Excludes is set when an --exclude flag is present: the copy leaves out
85		// paths the file names, so what it takes is no longer the whole of what it
86		// points at.
87		Excludes bool
88		// Sources are every argument but the destination, as written. Nil when the
89		// instruction could not be read — a malformed JSON form, a heredoc, a
90		// single argument — which a caller must read as "unknown", never as "copies
91		// nothing".
92		Sources []string
93	}

95	// TakesWholeContext reports whether the instruction copies the entire build
96	// context: its sources come from the context, one of them is the context's
97	// root, and no flag narrows it.
98	//
99	// Only the root itself counts — `.`, `./` and their cleaned equivalents. A glob
100	// such as `*` very probably takes everything too, but whether it matches dot
101	// files depends on the builder, and a check that fires on a guess about a
102	// builder is exactly the kind §3.81 rules out.
103	func (c Copy) TakesWholeContext() bool {
104		if c.From != "" || c.Excludes {
105			return false
106		}
107		for _, src := range c.Sources {
108			if path.Clean(strings.TrimSpace(src)) == "." {
109				return true
110			}
111		}
112		return false
113	}

146	func Parse(content []byte) File {
147		lines := splitLines(content)
148		esc := escapeChar(lines)
149	
150		var file File
151		args := map[string]argValue{}
152		names := map[string]bool{}
153		inStage := false
154	
155		for i := 0; i < len(lines); {
156			trimmed := strings.TrimSpace(lines[i].text)
157			if trimmed == "" || strings.HasPrefix(trimmed, "#") {
158				i++
159				continue
160			}
161			first := i
162			pieces, next := gather(lines, i, esc)
163			i = next
164			tokens := tokenize(pieces)
165			if len(tokens) == 0 {
166				continue
167			}
168			switch strings.ToUpper(tokens[0].text) {
169			case "ARG":
170				if !inStage {
171					readArgs(tokens[1:], args)
172				}
173			case "FROM":

192	}

197		cp := Copy{Keyword: strings.ToUpper(tokens[0].text)}
198		i := 1

200			k, v, _ := strings.Cut(tokens[i].text, "=")

206			}
207			i++
208		}

211			args = append(args, t.text)
212		}

214			// The JSON form. Joining on one space loses nothing that matters here:

216			var parts []string
217			if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(strings.Join(args, " ")), &parts); err != nil {
218				return cp
219			}
220			args = parts
221		}
222		if len(args) < 2 || strings.HasPrefix(args[0], "<<") {
223			return cp // a heredoc copies what the file spells, not the context
224		}
225		cp.Sources = args[:len(args)-1]
226		return cp
227	}

# entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)

You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.

## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)

Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:

    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"

Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.

## Hard rules

1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.
2. READ focused source around the result. Widen the check when aliases, generated code, dynamic
   dispatch, or related implementations could matter.
3. Use graph follow-ups only when they answer a real question. For impact or callers, prefer:
       entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X
4. Make the smallest complete edit and check sibling sites or contracts when the task implies them.
5. VERIFY before stopping. Run the most focused relevant test, build, or reproduction available.
   If execution is unavailable, perform a bounded source-level verification and state the limit.
6. Prefer precise queries and line ranges, but never trade resolution for fewer turns.
7. Feature-detect before relying on semantic relations:
       entire graph capabilities --json

## When NOT to use the graph

If the task already names the exact file and it is small, just read it — the graph saves tokens
by eliminating exploration; when there is nothing to explore, skip it.

## Reference

    locate  ->  entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "..."
    impact  ->  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X   (one shot: callers, callees, type consumers, data flow, co-change, siblings)
    callers ->  entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in

    detect  ->  entire graph capabilities --json   (inventory-only languages have no relations)
    stats   ->  entire graph stats --repo .        (human-facing token-savings report; not part of your workflow — do not run it unless asked)

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **AI Collaboration Rule**:
> - **Planning**, **Brainstorming**, **Implementation** and **Bug fixes** are all
>   in scope. Planning is no longer delegated to Gemini (Antigravity).
> - Implementation plans go in `.claude/plans/` (see
>   [rules/planning.md](rules/planning.md)); design decisions that outlive a plan
>   are recorded in `docs/backlog.md`.
> - Always refer to [project-context.md](../project-context.md) for global project rules.
>   It sits in this repository, at the root. The absolute path this line used to
>   carry named a GitLab checkout that is no longer where DevDesk lives.

## Project Overview

DevDesk is a terminal-based TUI (Text User Interface) application built with Go and Bubble Tea framework. It provides DevSecOps functionality including:
- System status monitoring (HTTP/HTTPS, ICMP, DNS, SSL checks)
- GitLab integration (authentication, project explorer, multi-select clone)
- Security scanning (Trivy CVE/secret/license/misconfig + Gitleaks secrets)
- Container management with real-time metrics, on Docker or Podman (`app.container_engine`)
- OCI resource management (image scanning, container launching, network inspection)
- Network diagnostics (DNS, route, ICMP, TCP, TLS, HTTP) + real-time port monitoring + this machine's interfaces + local port forwarding (unprivileged, loopback only)
- Multi-context configuration management via YAML
- Local workspaces management with git metadata

## Build and Development Commands

Tasks live in `mise.toml` — there is no Makefile. `mise tasks` lists them all.

```bash
# Development (fastest)
mise run dev          # Run directly with go run
go run .

# Build
mise run build        # Build binary to bin/dk
mise run run          # Build and run

# Testing
mise run test         # Run all tests
mise run cover        # Coverage per package
go test -v ./...      # Run all tests with verbose output
go test ./internal/command  # Run tests for specific package
mise run test-race    # Detect race conditions (critical for Bubble Tea Cmds)

# Code Quality
mise run fmt          # Format code
mise run vet          # Run go vet
mise run lint         # MANDATORY before commits - golangci-lint
mise run tidy         # Tidy dependencies
mise run check        # fmt + vet + lint + test in one go

# Installation
mise run install      # Install to $GOPATH/bin
```

`test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler (`gcc`/`clang`) on `PATH`.

## Work starts in a new worktree

**Any task that will produce a commit begins with its own worktree**, cut from
the current `main`, **under `.worktrees/` inside the repository**:

```bash
git fetch origin main
git worktree add -b <branch> .worktrees/<branch> origin/main
cd .worktrees/<branch>
```

Answering a question, reading code, running the app — none of that needs one.
Editing does.

**Under the repository, not beside it.** This reverses what this file said until
now, and the reason it gave was wrong. It claimed a worktree at `.worktrees/x`
would be compiled by `go build ./...` and `go test ./...`. It would not: the go
tool skips every directory whose name begins with `.` or `_`, so `.worktrees/`
is invisible to `./...`. Verified rather than assumed — a package of deliberately
invalid Go placed under `.worktrees/` builds clean and `go list ./...` does not
name it. The old argument holds for `worktrees/` without the dot, which is
presumably where it came from.

What decides it is the **sandbox mount**, and it cost a full debugging session to
find. A direct-mode sandbox mounts *this directory only*. A sibling worktree at
`../devdesk-<branch>` is therefore outside the mount, so its **files** are written
into the container's private layer and never reach the host — while `.git` is
inside the mount and stays shared. Refs agree, files diverge, and nothing warns:
the branch tip moves, the host's copy of those files does not, and `git status`
on the host reports the *stale* content as uncommitted modifications. An agent
and the person testing its work end up compiling different code while both
believe they are on the same branch. Under `.worktrees/`, host and sandbox see
one filesystem.

Two effects worth knowing, neither blocking:

- `.worktrees/` is in `.gitignore`; a worktree there is not a change to the tree.
- Claude Code discovers the nested `.claude/` of each worktree, so its skills and
  rules appear a second time, prefixed by the worktree path. Harmless, and the
  price of the directory being inside the repo.

**What isolates, and what does not.** git refuses to check out one branch in two
worktrees, so two agents cannot land on the same branch by accident — that is the
whole protection, and it is worth knowing what it does *not* cover:

| Shared by every worktree | Consequence |
|---|---|
| `~/.devdesk/` — contexts, `config.yaml`, scan caches | two agents editing settings or scanning at once overwrite each other's; nothing warns |
| the host keyring, Docker, the ports the app binds | one at a time, whoever gets there first |
| `.git/hooks` | verified: `git rev-parse --git-path hooks` resolves to the **main** checkout's, so the Entire checkpoint and pre-push hooks fire normally from a worktree |
| `origin` | inherited — `git push -u origin <branch>` goes through the mirror as usual |

`mise` tasks and `go build` work unchanged; both read the tree they are run in.

**`entire graph` indexes per directory.** A fresh worktree has no index, so the
first `entire graph search` there pays a full build (~5 s on this repo, measured)
and the symbol ids it returns are namespaced by the directory name
(`local/<branch>:Go:…`). Nothing breaks; do not be surprised by the first search
being slow or by ids that do not match another worktree's.

**Clean up when the PR is merged**, from the main checkout:

```bash
git worktree remove .worktrees/<branch>
git worktree list          # what is still out there
git worktree prune         # after a directory was deleted by hand
```

`git worktree remove` refuses a tree with uncommitted changes, which is the
point — look before forcing.

**The main checkout stays on `main` and stays clean.** It is what `git fetch
origin main && git merge --ff-only origin/main` needs after each merge, and what
every new worktree is cut from.

## Git workflow — pull requests only

**Never push directly to `main`.** The Entire mirror rejects it:

```
! [remote rejected] main -> main (protected branch)
```

This is enforced by the mirror, not by GitHub, and **Entire does not document it**
— neither the CLI help nor `docs.entire.io` mentions a protected default branch.
The only branch restriction Entire states is that `entire/unmirrored/*` is never
forwarded. Treat the rejection as observed behaviour, not as a specified one.

**The repository is public since 2026-09-06**, which is what makes GitHub-side
enforcement possible at all: a private repo on a free personal plan answers
`403 Upgrade to GitHub Pro or make this repository public` on both
`/repos/anthnel/devdesk/branches/main/protection` and
`/repos/anthnel/devdesk/rulesets` — that was the prior state, and it is not a
description to trust going forward if the repo ever goes private again. Do not
cite `gh api repos/anthnel/devdesk/branches/main` reporting `"protected":
false` as proof of anything either way: that field only ever reflects legacy
branch protection, so it reads `false` under a ruleset too, and it read `false`
on the free-private plan whatever the configuration. Query
`/repos/anthnel/devdesk/rulesets` itself (or `gh ruleset check main`) for the
real answer.

A ruleset named `main-protection` (id `22399372`) now targets `refs/heads/main`
only — deliberately not `entire/checkpoints/v1`, which receives automatic
pushes from the Entire hook and would break if rule-gated. It requires a pull
request (0 approving reviews — solo maintainer, the PR is a record not a review
gate) with the `Lint and build` and `Test` checks from `ci.yml` passing,
blocks force-pushes and branch deletion, and grants no bypass. This closes the
gap the mirror alone left open: the Entire mirror's rejection of a direct push
to `main` was, until now, the *only* protection — a second remote pointing
straight at GitHub would have sailed through (see the warning against adding
one, below). Now GitHub itself refuses that push too.

Every other branch, including `entire/checkpoints/v1`, pushes through the mirror
and is forwarded to GitHub.

**Pull requests are GitHub's, not Entire's.** Entire has no merge-request
concept — it layers checkpoints and sessions over git and forwards pushes. So
the PR steps below are `gh`, and the branch they review is one `origin` carried
to GitHub. `entire review` (labs) runs a multi-agent review against the current
branch and is a pre-merge step, not a substitute for the PR.

```bash
git worktree add -b <branch> .worktrees/<branch> origin/main   # work happens here
git push -u origin <branch>                     # via the mirror — forwarded to GitHub
gh pr create -R anthnel/devdesk --base main --head <branch>
gh pr merge -R anthnel/devdesk <n> --squash --delete-branch
# then, from the main checkout:
git fetch origin main && git merge --ff-only origin/main   # may need a retry, see below
git worktree remove .worktrees/<branch>
```

**`-R anthnel/devdesk` is not optional.** `gh` infers the repository from a
remote pointing at a GitHub host, and `origin` is an `entire://` URL, so it
finds none and fails with *"none of the git remotes configured for this
repository point to a known GitHub host"*. The flag names the repo directly.
Do not solve this by adding a GitHub remote — see below.

**After a merge, `origin` can read stale for a minute or two.** The mirror lags
GitHub, so `git fetch origin` right after `gh pr merge` may return the *previous*
`main` — with no error, which is the part that misleads. `gh pr view <n> --json state`
says `MERGED` while `git rev-parse origin/main` still points at the commit before
it. Re-run the fetch a moment later; `gh` is what to trust in the meantime,
because it talks to GitHub directly and needs no remote.

**Do not add a second remote pointing at GitHub to work around that.** The
`main-protection` ruleset (above) would now refuse a direct `git push github
main` too, so it is no longer the *only* defeat of the only protection — but a
direct push still bypasses the mirror, and with it the Entire hook that
records checkpoints and sessions, which is not visible until much later.
`origin` is the only remote, deliberately.

**Merging several branches cut from the same commit conflicts in
`docs/backlog.md`.** Every fix inserts its entry at the top of §1.1, so the
second and third merges land on the same anchor. The resolution is always to
keep both sides — they are independent entries, not competing edits.

### Landing a sandbox-made commit (host-relay)

A Docker Sandbox (`sbx`) has no `entire://` auth of its own — `ENTIRE_TOKEN`
via `sbx secret set-custom` doesn't work (`git-remote-entire` parses the
JWT's claims locally, before any network call, but the secret proxy only
substitutes the real token on the wire — the sandbox process itself only
ever sees an unparseable placeholder), and an interactive `entire login`
inside the sandbox trades that for a persistent, harder-to-reason-about
credential sitting in a less-trusted place. So the sandbox edits and commits
locally only; the host does every `origin` operation — fetch, push, PR,
merge. `git pull`/`git fetch` run *inside* the sandbox will fail with `no
auth context for cluster ...` — that's expected, not a setup bug; don't
`entire login` there to fix it (see `~/projects/github/anthnel/sbx-kits/entire/README.md`
for the full rationale).

A direct-mode sandbox mounts this exact repo directory, so both the commits and
the working files land where the host sees them — provided the worktree is under
`.worktrees/`, which is why that is the rule. There is nothing to transfer; the
host only has to push, because the sandbox has no `entire://` auth:

```bash
# From the host, once the sandbox reports "done and committed":
git push origin <branch>
gh pr create -R anthnel/devdesk --base main --head <branch> --fill
gh pr merge -R anthnel/devdesk <n> --squash --delete-branch
git fetch origin main && git merge --ff-only origin/main   # may need a retry, see above
git worktree remove .worktrees/<branch>
```

**If a worktree was made at the old sibling path** (`../devdesk-<branch>`), the
host cannot see its files and `git worktree list` shows it `prunable`. The
commits are still in the shared `.git/objects`, so nothing is lost — but the
host's copy of those files is stale, and `git status` there reports that stale
content as uncommitted modifications, which reads as if work were pending when
the opposite is true. Recover by taking the branch tip:

```bash
git stash push -m "stale files from a sandbox sibling worktree"   # reversible
git worktree prune -v                  # drop the unreachable admin entry
git push origin <sha>:refs/heads/<branch>
```

**A worktree created from inside the sandbox registers a Linux path the
host's git can't resolve — even under `.worktrees/`.** `.worktrees/` shares
*files* between host and sandbox, but each side's git still writes its own
`.git/worktrees/<name>/gitdir` pointer, and the sandbox's git records a Linux
path (`/c/Users/...`). The host's `git worktree remove` on that same
directory then fails with `fatal: '<path>' is not a working tree` — Windows
git cannot resolve the pointer left behind. The costlier part: a plain `git
worktree prune` run on the host right after that failure deregisters the
worktree **silently** — git treats an unresolvable pointer as a worktree
that's gone — while leaving alone any sibling worktree whose path it *can*
read. If the branch was already merged the content is safe either way, but a
host-run `prune` while an agent is still working inside a sandbox-created
worktree would deregister that worktree out from under it, mid-task, with
nothing on either side raising a warning. The rule this implies: **whoever
creates a worktree removes it** — do not `git worktree remove` or `prune`
from the other side of the host/sandbox split.

#### Developing in the sandbox, testing from the host

This is the normal mode, and the split works out well: **git is what the
host does not need in the worktree, the build is what the sandbox does not
need.** Measured in a worktree whose pointer carries a Linux path, from the
host:

| From the host, in `.worktrees/<branch>/` | Result |
|---|---|
| any `git` command | `fatal: not a git repository: (NULL)` |
| `go build ./...` | exit 0 |
| `go test ./internal/command/` | `ok … 0.239s` |
| `go build .` (with buildvcs stamping) | exit 0 |
| `mise run build` | OK |

The breakage is therefore **entirely** on the git side, not just on
`worktree remove`: Go does not need the VCS, and `-buildvcs=auto` degrades
silently rather than failing when it gets no answer. The main checkout is
never affected.

The resulting split of responsibilities:

1. **The sandbox creates the worktree** — it is the one that will commit
   into it, so it is the one that must keep a working git.
2. **The sandbox edits and commits.** All the git activity happens there.
3. **The host builds, tests, and runs the application** in that same
   directory, since the files are shared through the mount. No git command
   here — the `fatal` above is expected, it does not signal a broken repo.
4. **To read the diff from the host, go through the main checkout**: the
   refs and `.git/objects` are shared, so it sees everything the sandbox
   committed — `git log --oneline main..<branch>`, `git diff main...<branch>`.
5. **The host pushes and merges from the main checkout**, never from the
   worktree — that is the host-relay above.
6. **The sandbox removes its worktree.** If it no longer exists, the host can
   delete the *files* (they are inside the mount, unlike the sibling case
   above) then `git worktree prune` — but only once no sandbox still has a
   live worktree.

**Testing from the host is not a workaround.** DevDesk needs a real
terminal, the host's Docker socket, the host's secret manager
(`internal/credentials`), `~/.devdesk/`, and binding ports: none of that is
representative inside the sandbox. What the sandbox does better is write
code.

**The reverse direction is forbidden**: the host does not create the
worktree for the sandbox to work in. By symmetry, the `C:/Users/...` path
Windows git writes is not resolvable under Linux — the sandbox would lose
the git it needs to commit. (This direction has not been tested; it is the
same mechanism read backwards.)

**A follow-up commit on the same branch, after the first one already got
squash-merged, will conflict on a plain `git merge`** — squashing rewrites
history, so `git merge origin/main` computes the wrong common ancestor
(the branch's *own* pre-squash parent) and re-diffs files that already
landed, even when nothing actually conflicts in substance. Don't hand-edit
through that; cherry-pick the new commit straight onto current `origin/main`
instead — its real parent already matches what's on `main`, so it applies
clean:

```bash
git worktree add -b <tmp-branch> .worktrees/<tmp-branch> <new-sha>
cd .worktrees/<tmp-branch>
git reset --hard origin/main
git cherry-pick <new-sha>              # clean apply — verify before trusting this
go build ./... && go test ./<touched-packages>/...
git push origin HEAD:refs/heads/<new-branch-name>
# gh pr create / gh pr merge as above, then from the main checkout:
git worktree remove .worktrees/<tmp-branch>
```

### Publishing a release — release-please, then goreleaser

**A release takes two merges, and that is the point.** `release-please`
watches `main` and keeps a **release pull request** open: it reads the
conventional commits since the last tag, decides the version, and writes
`CHANGELOG.md`. Merging that PR creates the tag and the GitHub Release;
`goreleaser` then builds the six binaries (linux, darwin, windows × amd64,
arm64) and attaches them to that Release.

#### The flow, plainly — accumulate, then release whenever you want

The two actors: `release-please` **proposes** (it never writes directly to
`main` except through its own PR), `goreleaser` **builds**, and it only
triggers once that PR is merged. Concrete timeline:

1. A `fix:` or a `feat:` is merged onto `main` (a normal work PR, see
   above). The code ships right away. release-please sees that commit and
   **creates or updates** — never two PRs in parallel — the
   "chore(main): release x.y.z" PR with the corresponding changelog; that PR
   only touches `CHANGELOG.md` and `.release-please-manifest.json`.
2. Step 1 repeats as many times as wanted — several fixes, one or several
   features, over days or weeks. Each merge grows the same release PR (the
   version number can climb, a `feat:` bumps the minor) without any tag
   being set and without any binary being published.
3. When the moment is judged right — and only then — the release PR itself
   gets merged. That specific merge, and only that one, sets the tag,
   creates the GitHub Release, and wakes up goreleaser.

| Action | Effect |
|---|---|
| Merge a `fix:`/`feat:` onto `main` | Code shipped immediately; the release PR updates in the background; nothing is published |
| Merge the release PR | **Sole trigger for publishing** — tag, Release, binaries |

Publishing is therefore never a per-commit act: it is a deliberate act,
decided by merging a PR that already exists and that can be left to grow
indefinitely.

```bash
# nothing to run: the release PR opens and updates itself on its own
gh pr list -R anthnel/devdesk --label "autorelease: pending"
gh pr merge -R anthnel/devdesk <n> --squash   # ← this merge is what publishes
```

**Why not semantic-release**, which would achieve the same thing in a single
merge: it pushes the tag directly to `main`, and this repository forbids
that — the Entire mirror rejects that push, and this refusal is the *only*
protection `main` has, since branch protection is unavailable on this plan
(the 403 above). One extra merge per release is the price of that rule.

**The mirror replicates tags, verified on 2026-09-06.** The tag is set by
GitHub Actions, so it is born on GitHub and not via the mirror — but
`git fetch origin --tags` brings it back, just as it brings back a
squash-merge done by `gh`. That was the only unknown in the chain, and it is
now resolved: nothing forces setting a tag by hand.

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `release-please-config.json` | the type (`go`), the CHANGELOG sections |
| `.release-please-manifest.json` | the current version — **written by the bot**, never by hand |
| `.goreleaser.yaml` | the six targets, the `-ldflags`, `mode: append` |
| `.github/workflows/release.yml` | the two jobs, chained by `release_created` |

**A repository setting no workflow can grant itself**: *Settings →
Actions → Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests*. Without
it, the first run fails on the PR it cannot open, and the message does not
say that is why. **Already active here** —
`gh api repos/anthnel/devdesk/actions/permissions/workflow` answers
`can_approve_pull_request_reviews: true`, verified on 2026-09-06. The same
call shows `default_workflow_permissions: read`, which is not a problem:
that is the default when a workflow states nothing, and `release.yml`
declares its own.

**The binary's version comes from `-ldflags`**, not from a committed file
(§3.62). `release-please` knows how to write into a Go file (`versionFile`)
and it is not used for that: it would be a second source of truth for an
answer the build already gives, and a dev binary would then show the number
of the last release instead of `dev`.

**Before pushing a change to the chain**, `mise run release-check` validates
the configuration and `mise run release-snapshot` builds the six targets
without publishing anything — it is the only way to discover a broken target
before a tag is set.

**The first release will list the whole history** (66 `feat:` and 50 `fix:`
as of 2026-09-06). This is deliberate — an empty first CHANGELOG would be
worse — and the PR is editable before the merge. To start at `1.0.0` rather
than `0.1.0`, a one-off `"release-as": "1.0.0"` in the config, removed
afterward.

### Remotes

| Remote | URL | Use |
|--------|-----|-----|
| `origin` | `entire://aws-eu-central-1.entire.io/gh/anthnel/devdesk` | Entire mirror — everything: clone, fetch, push |

**There is one remote, and there should stay one.** The repository is hosted on
GitHub and mirrored to EntireDB in `aws-eu-central-1` (a second placement exists
in `aws-us-east-2`), but every git operation goes through the mirror: it is the
regional path, it is what keeps agent reads fast, and it is where the checkpoint
hook runs. Anything needing GitHub's own answer — PR state, review threads —
goes through `gh`, which authenticates directly and does not need a remote.

Semantic search (`entire search`, and the `entire:*` skills that depend on it) is
**not available in the EU region** — the server answers `semantic search is not
yet available in the region(s) hosting this search`. Nothing in the repo config
fixes this.

## Architecture

The deep notes live in `docs/architecture/`, one file per area, and they are
**not** `@`-imported: an `@` would inline all of it into every session, which is
the thing this split exists to avoid. Read the file that covers what you are
touching, and update it in the same commit as the code.

| File | Covers |
|---|---|
| [`app-shell.md`](../docs/architecture/app-shell.md) | the router and its views, `ctrl+p` and the command parser, the keyboard vocabulary (`internal/ui/keymap`), greyed shortcuts, `shared.State`, cross-view messages, the jobs registry (`internal/jobs`), the one spinner chain and the `:jobs` view |
| [`configuration.md`](../docs/architecture/configuration.md) | the config schema, the contexts, the migrations (`gitlab:` → `forge:`, `docker:` → `network:`), and the configuration view |
| [`forge.md`](../docs/architecture/forge.md) | `internal/forge` and its two backends, `forge.Vocabulary`, and the explorer's clone pipeline |
| [`workspaces.md`](../docs/architecture/workspaces.md) | the `ws` file icons (`internal/ui/fileicon`) and the sync (`F`) |
| [`viewer.md`](../docs/architecture/viewer.md) | `internal/viewer` + `internal/ui/viewer` — kinds, displays, colouring, search, follow |
| [`scanning.md`](../docs/architecture/scanning.md) | Trivy, Gitleaks, plumber, `scan.Categorize`, the `:sec` inventory, the two scan caches |
| [`registries.md`](../docs/architecture/registries.md) | the registry/group model and the discovered-members cache |
| [`network.md`](../docs/architecture/network.md) | `internal/docker` and `internal/oci`, the netdiag view, `internal/ports`, `internal/netiface` |
| [`mcp.md`](../docs/architecture/mcp.md) | the MCP server the TUI serves over HTTP |
| [`templates.md`](../docs/architecture/templates.md) | `internal/template` + `internal/ui/templates` — the repository-template catalog, its three sources, how files are fetched, and the `:templates` view |
| [`ui-components.md`](../docs/architecture/ui-components.md) | `components.FooterMessage` and `internal/ui/datatable` |

### Status Monitoring System

**Factory Pattern for Checkers:**
- `internal/status/checker.go` - Main orchestrator
- `internal/status/http_checker.go` - HTTP/HTTPS checks
- `internal/status/icmp_checker.go` - ICMP ping checks
- `internal/status/dns_checker.go` - DNS resolution checks

Each checker implements `CheckerInterface`. The main `Checker.CheckOne()` uses a factory pattern to instantiate the right checker based on `component.Type`.

**Parallel Execution:**
- `CheckAll()` runs all component checks concurrently using goroutines and sync.WaitGroup
- Results are collected and returned as `[]ComponentStatus`

### Component CRUD Operations

Status view supports adding/editing/deleting monitors:
- `internal/ui/status/components/component_form.go` - Form component
- `internal/ui/status/components/confirm_modal.go` - Confirmation dialog
- Changes persist to `~/.devdesk/config.yaml` via `config.Save()`

State flags in Model: `creating`, `editing`, `confirming`, `selectedIdx`

### Credentials Management

No secret DevDesk holds is written to a file DevDesk owns. `internal/credentials`
implements the `Storage` interface three ways and `Select()` picks exactly one —
writing to several at once is what let the old "secure" option store a token in
the credential manager *and* in plaintext:

| Storage | Backend | Notes |
|---------|---------|-------|
| `KeyringStorage` | Windows Credential Manager / macOS Keychain / Secret Service | via `zalando/go-keyring`, no cgo. The default. |
| `GitCredentialStorage` | git's configured credential helper | Only when the helper is not `store`, which writes plaintext. Context-aware. |
| `MemoryStorage` | this process | Last resort, and deliberately worse: the auth view says nothing was saved. |

`Select(context, preference)` returns a `Selection{Storage, Backend, Detail}`.
The order is keyring → git credential → memory; `app.secret_backend` in the
context config pins the head of it (`auto`, `keyring`, `git-credential`). A
pinned backend that is unreachable falls through to memory rather than silently
to the other one.

The router resolves one `Selection` per context and keeps it in
`shared.State.Secrets`. It must be reused for the lifetime of the context — a
second `Select()` call yields a fresh `MemoryStorage` that cannot see what the
first one holds.

`MigrateLegacySecrets` runs at startup and on every context switch: a
`gitlab.token` or `registry.password` left in a context file by an older build
is moved into the store and deleted from the YAML, with the result reported in
the auth view.

## Testing

Test files follow Go conventions (`*_test.go`):
- `internal/command/parser_test.go` - Command parser tests
- `internal/app/app_test.go` - App router tests

Use table-driven tests where appropriate.

## Dependencies

Key libraries (see `go.mod`):
- `github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea` - TUI framework
- `github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles` - Pre-built TUI components (table, textinput, spinner)
- `github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss` - Styling
- `gitlab.com/gitlab-org/api/client-go` - GitLab API client
- `github.com/prometheus-community/pro-bing` - ICMP ping functionality (maintained fork of go-ping/ping)
- `github.com/google/go-github/v68` - GitHub API client (§3.6)
- `github.com/libp2p/go-netroute` - which interface a destination leaves by, on all three platforms (§3.44)
- `github.com/zalando/go-keyring` - host secret manager (wincred / Keychain / Secret Service), no cgo
- `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` - YAML configuration

## Code Conventions

- Comments: **English only** (Rule 307) — existing French comments are not rewritten wholesale, but any new or edited comment is in English
- Commit messages: **English only** (Rule 307)
- UI text and logs: **English US only** (Rule 129)
- Bubbletea models define their own message types
- Use `theme` package for consistent styling (`internal/ui/theme/`)
- Config changes must call `config.Save()` to persist
- All colors defined in `theme/colors.go`, all styles in `theme/styles.go`
- Message naming: `[ComponentName][Action]Msg` (e.g., `ComponentFormSubmitMsg`)

## Critical Bubble Tea Rules

**NEVER modify model state inside a Cmd** (Rule 110) - Race condition:
- `Update()` is the ONLY place to modify model state
- `View()` is read-only
- `Cmd` functions do I/O and return messages

**NEVER use `style.Render()` inside `table.Row{}`** (Rule 122) - ANSI sequences corrupt all subsequent rows:
- Use plain text: `theme.IconError + " error"` not `theme.StatusErrorStyle.Render(...)`
- Apply row styling via `table.SetStyles(theme.TableStylesForState("error"))`

**Update() case extraction**: If a case block exceeds 5 lines, extract to `handle[MessageType]()` method returning `(tea.Model, tea.Cmd)`

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.
